Text.name: task_instructions
Text.value:
Your goal is to extract the following entities from the methods section of a scientific article (visible on the left). While questions will appear throughout the full text for qualitative annotation, the end goal is quantitative annotation:
• SAMPLE: Total unique participants (humans)
• N MALE: Total unique male participants
• N FEMALE: Total unique female participants
Optional:
• % MALE: Percentage of male participants
• % FEMALE: Percentage of female participants
Be accurate and meticulous when annotating the total number of participants, to the best of your knowledge.
If the information is not explicitly stated or if there is any ambiguity, prioritize selecting 'Unclear' rather than making assumptions or guesses.

Header.value: 1. Does the text involve research on humans or human samples?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q1
Text.value:
🔍 What to look for:
- Participants, subjects, patients, volunteers
- Human samples (blood, tissue, etc.)
- Survey respondents or interview subjects
❌ Select 'No' if:
- Cell lines only
- Purely animal studies
❓ Select 'Unclear' if:
- The text is confusing or lacks enough information to determine whether human subjects or samples are involved.

Header.value: 2: Does the text involve only one sex or gender?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q2
Text.value:
🔍 Response Options:
- ✅ Yes – Biologically Sex-Specific: The text exclusively involves one biological sex due to inherent biological reasons.
- Examples: Prostate cancer (affects males), ovarian cancer (affects females), menstrual disorders (affects females).
- 🔍 Yes – Contextually Justified: The text focuses on one sex or gender for valid contextual or research reasons, even if the condition can affect both sexes.
- Examples: Research on breast cancer (primarily affects females), male-pattern baldness (primarily affects males), domestic violence against women, workplace injuries in male-dominated industries.
- ⚠️ Yes – Not Justified: The text involves only one sex or gender without a clear or valid reason for excluding the other.
- 👥 No – Both Sexes: The text includes participants of both sexes or genders.
- ❓ Unclear: The text does not specify the sex of gender of participants, or it is unclear whether one of both are involved.

Header.value: 3. Does the text contain quantitative data, i.e., SAMPLE and/or N FEMALES, N MALES, %FEMALE, %MALE?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q3
Text.value:
✅ Yes – Individual Participants: The text provides quantitative data on the number of distinct participants in the study, either overall, by sex/gender or by subgroups. Examples:
- '150 participants,' 'n=45,' or 'cohort of 2,847 patients.'
- '65 women and 85 men,' '18 males and 22 females.'
- '23 patients with diabetes,' 'control group (n=30).'
- '65% female', '40% of participants.'
⚠️ Yes – Multiple Samples per Individual: The text includes quantitative data, but it refers to multiple measurements or samples from the same participants without disclosing total number of participants. (E.g. '50 samples from lung tissue')
❌ No: There is no quantitative information of any of the variables of interest (SAMPLE, N FEMALES, N MALES, %FEMALE, %MALE).
❓ Unclear: It is not clear whether the text contains any quantitative data about these variables.

Header.value: 5: Is the total quantitative data for variable SAMPLE explicitly stated without requiring additional calculations?

Choice.value: No, I need to do implicit calculations

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q5_sample
Text.value:
✅ Yes:
- The total SAMPLE is explicitly stated, requiring no additional calculations to determine the total.
- Examples: 'The are 100 participants'.
❌ No (Implicit Data):
- The data requires further calculations or interpretation to determine the total SAMPLE. This may occur with complex reporting structures or incomplete data.
- Example 1: The case study detailed the medical histories of three individual patients: John, a 45-year-old male; Mary, a 50-year-old female; and Alex, a 60-year-old male. Their treatment responses were monitored individually. Here total SAMPLE=1+1+1.
- Example 2: The study analyzed 60 patients with diabetes who were following a treatment regimen, 50 patients who were not following the treatment, and 40 patients who served as a control group. Here total SAMPLE=60+50+40.
❓ Unclear: It is not clear whether the text contains explicit SAMPLEuantitative data about these variables.

Header.value: 6. Are there dropouts mentioned in the text?

Choice.value: Yes, Before the start of the study, in the recruitment stage

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q6
Text.value:
• ✅ Yes, Before the Start of the Study (Recruitment Stage): Dropouts are explicitly mentioned as occurring during recruitment, before the study began. Examples: '10 participants dropped out before the study began', or 'Several individuals decided not to participate during the initial recruitment'.
• ✅ Yes, After the Study Started: Dropouts are mentioned as occurring after the study had commenced. Examples: '5 participants withdrew after the first session', or 'Some subjects were lost to follow-up during the study.'
• ❓ Unclear:It is not clear whether dropouts are mentioned or when they occurred. The text may be ambiguous or lacking detail.
• ❌ No: There is no mention of dropouts in the text.

Header.value: 7: Does the study include multiple participant groups, detailed breakdowns, or individual-level analysis?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q7
Text.value:
• ✅ Yes: The study includes disaggregated data, such as:
- Multiple cohorts or groups, e.g. 'The study analyzed 60 patients with diabetes who were following a treatment regimen, 50 patients who were not following the treatment, and 40 patients who served as a control group'.
- Individual-level data, e.g., The case study detailed the medical histories of three individual patients: John, a 45-year-old male; Mary, a 50-year-old female; and Alex, a 60-year-old male. Their treatment responses were monitored individually.
- A matching ratio, e.g., A 1:1 matching ratio was used for cases and controls,
• ❌ No: The study does not feature multiple cohorts, disaggregated data, individual-level data, or a matching ratio.
• ❓ Unclear: It is not clear whether the study includes these elements. The text may lack detail or be ambiguous.

Header.value: 8: Is it necessary to infer SAMPLE, N FEMALE, or N MALE using one or more of the following methods?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q8
Text.value:
• ✔️ Sample + One Sex: Use subtraction if the total SAMPLE and one sex count are provided.
Example: 'Given SAMPLE = 150, N FEMALE = 80; infer N MALE as 150 - 80 = 70'.
• ✔️ Both Sexes: Use addition if counts for both sexes are provided.
Example: 'Given N FEMALE = 80, N MALE = 70; infer SAMPLE as 80 + 70 = 150'.
• ✔️ Sample + One Sex Percentage: Use percentage if total SAMPLE and a percentage for one sex are known.
Example: 'Given SAMPLE = 150, 60% female; infer N FEMALE as 60% of 150 = 90'.
• ❌ None of the Above: None of these methods are needed to determine the SAMPLE, N FEMALE and/or N MALE.
• ❓ Unclear: Insufficient information to determine if these methods are applicable.

Header.value: 9: Is it straightforward to infer total [SAMPLE], OR the combined total [SAMPLE = N FEMALES + N MALES] using the available data?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q9
Text.value:
🔍 How to Determine Inference Clarity:
• ✔️ Yes: The data needed to calculate the total SAMPLE, N FEMALE, or N MALE is clearly presented, allowing for straightforward calculations.
Example: 'Fifteen healthy human volunteers took part in the study. Two were later excluded. Therefore, data from 13 participants (10 female; mean age 27 years) were included in the analysis'.
Explanation: The study provides the initial SAMPLE minus dropouts, resulting in SAMPLE = 13, with N FEMALE = 10 explicitly mentioned. N MALE can be calculated as 13 - 10 = 3.
• ❌ No: The data is not presented in a way that allows for straightforward calculations of the total SAMPLE, N FEMALE, or N MALE.
• ❓ Unclear: It is not clear whether the available data allows for straightforward calculations. The text provides some numbers, but it is ambiguous whether they represent total values or subsets.

Header.style: background-color: white; padding: 10px; margin: 25px 0 10px 0; font-weight: bold;

Text.name: q9_calc
Text.value:
📊 Calculating Totals:
• Total SAMPLE: Sum of all individual sample groups (e.g., SAMPLE = SAMPLE1 + SAMPLE2 + ...)
• Total N FEMALE: Sum of all female participants across groups
• Total N MALE: Sum of all male participants across groups
🔍 Other Calculation Possibilities:
• Adjusted SAMPLE due to dropouts: total SAMPLE = Initial SAMPLE – Dropouts
• Both sexes: SAMPLE = N FEMALE + N MALE
• Inferring One Sex: N_SEX2 = SAMPLE - N_SEX1
% Percentage Calculations:
• ⚠️ Use only when no raw counts are available.
• Possible Calculations:
N_SEX1 = SAMPLE * % SEX1
% SEX2 = 100 - % SEX1

Header.value: 10. Can some numbers still be annotated reasonably, even if SAMPLE ≠ N FEMALE + N MALE?

View.style: background-color: #e7f3ff; padding: 10px; margin: 5px 0; border-left: 3px solid #007bff; border-radius: 3px;

Text.name: q10
Text.value:
🔍 How to Determine Annotation Feasibility:
• ✔️ Yes: Even if the total SAMPLE does not equal the sum of N FEMALE and N MALE, other numbers can still be reasonably annotated.
Example: ‘Twenty-seven subjects (ten female) diagnosed with an ASD participated in this study. Additionally, fifteen typical adults served as controls’.
Explanation: Here, although SAMPLE does not directly equal the sum of N FEMALE and N MALE due to unknown information, we can annotate SAMPLE = 27 + 15 = 42, N FEMALE = 10, and N MALE = 17, as the sex of the control group is not specified.
• ❌ No: Numbers cannot be reasonably annotated due to insufficient or unclear data. It is too difficult to annotate either SAMPLE, N FEMALE, or N MALE.
• ❓ Unclear: It is not clear whether numbers can be reasonably annotated for some participants in the text.

Header.style: background-color: white; padding: 10px; margin: 25px 0 10px 0; font-weight: bold;

Text.value:
📊 Calculating Totals:
• Total SAMPLE: Sum of all individual sample groups (e.g., SAMPLE = SAMPLE1 + SAMPLE2 + ...)

• Possible Calculations:

% SEX2 = 100 - % SEX1
